readerTitle: Why "5% off for cash" beats "5% extra for card"
caseNote: 실제 연구 (Thaler 1980, Tversky & Kahneman 1981, Gourville 1998) + 가상 사례 (가구 매장, 화물 운송사, 소프트웨어 요금제) · 사례 수치는 모두 설명용
insight: 가격은 숫자가 아니라 표현으로 느껴진다. 같은 돈이라도 단위, 기간, 이득인지 손실인지에 따라 고객의 반응이 달라지므로, 비용은 작게 보이고 이득은 크게 보이도록 정직하게 표현을 고른다.
misconception: 돈이 똑같으면 어떻게 보여 주든 고객의 반응도 같다. 가격 표현은 꾸밈일 뿐 결정에는 영향이 없다.

sources.text: Thaler, R. (1980). Toward a Positive Theory of Consumer Choice. Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, 1(1), 39–60.
Tversky, A. & Kahneman, D. (1981). The Framing of Decisions and the Psychology of Choice. Science, 211(4481), 453–458.
Gourville, J. T. (1998). Pennies-a-Day: The Effect of Temporal Reframing on Transaction Evaluation. Journal of Consumer Research, 24(4), 395–408.
가구 매장, 화물 운송사, 소프트웨어 요금제 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Thaler(1980)가 신용카드 업계가 현금·카드 가격 차이를 '카드 추가 요금'이 아니라 '현금 할인'으로 표현하도록 선호했다고 쓴 내용을 원문에서 확인하세요. 카드에는 연구 결과가 아니라 업계 관찰로 적었습니다.
Tversky & Kahneman(1981)의 재킷·계산기 실험: 싼 물건에서 $5를 아끼려고 다른 매장까지 가겠다는 응답이 비싼 물건보다 많았다는 내용입니다. 카드에는 정확한 가격과 비율을 쓰지 않고 일반적으로 묘사했습니다.
Gourville(1998)의 '하루 몇 센트' 표현 효과는 일반적으로만 묘사했습니다. 효과의 크기와 조건(작은 금액에서 주로 작동)을 원문에서 확인하세요.
카드 추가 요금(서차지)은 나라와 지역마다 규제가 다릅니다. 레슨에서는 법률 조언 없이 '규칙이 지역마다 다르다'고만 언급했습니다.

cards.title: Same lamp. Same money. Different mood.
body: Two shops sell the same lamp. Shop one tags it $100 and gives $5 off for cash. Shop two tags it $95 and adds $5 if you pay by card.
A card customer pays $100 in both shops. A cash customer pays $95 in both. Not one cent is different.
Yet one of these shops is far more likely to hear grumbling at the register. Can you guess which?

image.label: Two identical lamps with different price tags
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 똑같은 스탠드 조명 두 개가 나란히 있고, 왼쪽 가격표에는 "$100 · $5 off for cash"(초록색 리본), 오른쪽 가격표에는 "$95 · +$5 for card"(빨간색 경고 표시). 실제 브랜드나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Card fees are eating your margin.
body: You run a furniture store. Card processing fees cost you about 3% on most sales, and most customers pay by card.
You want to recover that cost. What do you do?

options.feedback: No friction at the register, but cash customers now pay for card fees and you lose any way to nudge people toward cheaper payments.

options.text: Show the card price as the normal price and offer a small discount for cash
options.feedback: Card payers see the normal price, and cash payers feel they won something. Same money as a surcharge, but nobody feels fined.

options.text: Keep prices and add a 3% card surcharge at checkout
options.feedback: It recovers the fee exactly, but it appears at the last moment as a penalty. That's when customers feel cheated and walk away.

cards.title: A lost dollar hurts more than a missed one.
body: Research by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky showed that people feel a loss more sharply than a gain of the same size.
A surcharge is a loss: *you pay extra*. A cash discount is a missed gain: *you didn't save*. Same $5, different pain.

Economist Richard Thaler noted in 1980 that the card industry preferred stores to describe the gap as a "cash discount" rather than a "card surcharge". They understood that the label shapes how customers react.

cards.title: Price framing
body: **Price framing** is how you describe a price: the unit, the time period, and whether it reads as a gain or a loss. The frame changes how the price feels, even when the money is identical.
The lamp shops didn't differ in price. They differed in frame. One gave a gift. The other charged a fine.

image.label: One price shown through four different frames
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 가운데 동전 더미 "$365" 하나에서 네 개의 액자가 뻗어 나옴: "$1 a day", "$365 a year", "Save 10%", "Save $40". 같은 돈이 다른 액자 속에서 크기가 다르게 보이는 느낌. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Four frames you choose every time you quote.
body: Every price comes with a frame, chosen or not. The main levers:
list: **Gain or loss:** a discount for one option feels better than a fee for the other
**Time:** "under $1 a day" feels smaller than "$300 a year", as John Gourville's research on pennies-a-day framing showed
**Percent or amount:** people will travel to save $5 on a cheap item but not on an expensive one
**Separate or combined:** a cost folded into a bigger saving stings less than a cost on its own
cards.callout: Rule of thumb: let costs look small and savings look big, using true numbers.

cards.title: The same idea on a software pricing page.
body: A project tool costs $29 a month, or $290 if paid yearly instead of $348.
"Save 17%" and "2 months free" describe the exact same deal. Many teams find the second one lands better, because free months feel like a gift you can picture.
The reverse works for costs. A $348 yearly plan reads heavier than "$29 a month", even for a buyer who knows the math.

cards.title: A frame can't rescue a bad price.
body: Framing changes how a fair price feels. It won't make an overpriced product worth buying, and buyers who calculate, especially business buyers, will see the total anyway.

Frames that hide the real cost backfire. Fees revealed at checkout or savings that need small print make customers feel tricked, and that distrust lasts longer than the sale. Rules on surcharges and price displays also vary by place.
Pick the clearest true frame, not the cleverest one.

cards.title: Now it's a trucking company.
body: You haul 50,000 pallets a year for a retail client. Rising costs force a rate increase of $0.60 per pallet, or $30,000 a year.
At the same time, you've found a way to combine their shipments that saves them $90,000 a year. How do you open the proposal?

options.text: "Rates rise just $0.60 per pallet, and consolidation saves you $90,000 a year"
options.feedback: Each number is framed in your favor, but the increase still stands alone as a loss. Mixing units can also look like spin to a buyer who runs the totals.

options.text: "Rates rise $30,000 a year. Consolidation saves you $1.80 per pallet"
options.feedback: This makes the cost loud and the saving tiny. The client's first reaction will be to fight the increase.

options.text: "With the new rate and consolidation, you save $60,000 a year, or $1.20 per pallet"
options.feedback: The increase is folded into a larger gain, so it never reads as a loss on its own. Show the full breakdown below so the buyer can check it.

cards.softwareNote: The same move works for a price increase on a subscription: lead with the new feature's value and the net result, then show the old and new price clearly underneath.

cards.title: The same price can feel like a gift or a fine.
body: Customers react to how a price is described, not just to the number. Choose the unit, the time period and the gain-or-loss frame on purpose, and keep every number true.
**Try it today:** take one price you quote often. Write it three ways: per day or per use, as a yearly total, and as a saving instead of a cost. Which is both honest and easiest to say yes to?
